title: Goodbye, Love That Remains...
text:
Goodbye, love that remains,

asleep and naked to the wind;

footprints in your alleyways

will prolong my daydreams,

footprints inside the soul

will cultivate your memory;

goodbye, my land of love,

asleep and naked to the wind.


Of the vast world, of the world,

I now have and want nothing;

but guarded in the mountains

there is a corner of silence,

an intoxication for the eyes,

an anxiety for the breast,

and a song for the lips

that waits for me at all times.


And I must return and return

like the traveling pendulum,

and as the girl returns

when she looks at herself in the mirror.

Silence of my mountains,

Pátzcuaro of double sky,

I must return and return

like the traveling pendulum!
editorial_note: The translation keeps Urquiza's farewell to Pátzcuaro as a pendulum-like promise of return.

title: Because to Love, to Suffer...
text:
because to love, to suffer

        is a certain sign,

and silence the purest sacrifice,

and where

        love always finds merit.


To die in one's passion without declaring it

is the true

        office of one who loves,

for a silent weeping as exercise

gives more reason for itself,

        not daring to give it.


Whoever is silent while loving dies loving alone,

for the one who manages

        to speak himself is no care;

one says less and loves more when one loves most.


Because if my silence has not spoken to you,

I do not know how to tell you more than this: if

        I should die,

what I have kept silent has told you enough.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the damaged indentation and the conceit that silence itself speaks love.

title: To Vain Hopes of the Court
text:
Medinilla tires me out riding jineta,

        and Hijar rots me riding bridle-style;

        Don Zárate finishes off my life

        because he follows Tello's vile sect.


        Franqueza has begged me to put him

        in a sonnet, since everyone knows

        his foolish gravity, all born

        from not remembering that he was a soleta.


        Don Rodrigo de Tapia, the empty fool,

        never quite manages to know, vague ignorance,

        which is the right-hand side in his carriage.


        He is a gentleman of importance

        and has a certain grace: in summer

        from his armpit he gives off great fragrance.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the court satire's named targets, riding jokes, and deliberately crude final insult.

title: To an Academy Held in the House of Antonio de Vega, a Converso
text:
News of the great council reaches me,

        and that they are moving the Jordan to Italy;

        take care, Apollo, for impious people

        fear the flames and are blinded by the light.


        Let Antonio de Vega be an academic

        in your Judaizing company,

        and no longer Vega of the Ave Maria,

        but of the base tribe that denies it.


        From such a Maecenas, then, from a gathered

        Judaic rabble, Toledo now expects

        new flames and Christ another lance-thrust.


        Much light and little wax is promised me

        by people who, confessed as conversos,

        will give us their bonfire for illuminations.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the historical satire's hostile anti-converso language as source context, without endorsing it.

title: On Withdrawal from the Ambitions of the Court
text:
If there is sanctuary for the ill-contented,

        let the soul's sweet quiet be so

        in this solitude, where care harvests

        counsel and not fatigue.


        Let the one who, flattered by courtly pomp,

        still flatters himself with deceits,

        see metal loosened in rain

        fall upon an ambitious hand.


        Let sirens be the flattery of his mud,

        which, adulterating the keys of reason,

        close the door of better sense.


        I, among these gentle waves, to the birds,

        in song neither flattered nor learned,

        will owe the denial of grave fatigues.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the poem's retreat from court ambition into solitude, waves, and unlearned birdsong.
